A clutch type no-spin differential stops one wheel from spinning uncontrollably by using friction clutches to lock the axles together whenever one drive wheel experiences uncontrolled slippage. Specifically, the multiple plate clutch type uses four side gear pinions on two shafts that are at right angles to each other. These shafts engage similar V-shaped slots in the differential case. Each side gear is backed by a series of multiple disk clutches. When one wheel is turning faster than the other, the faster-turning splined side member and driven clutch member cause the ramps on the center cam and driven clutch member cam to push the driven clutch member away from the spider. This action is similar to the operation of other no-spin differentials. The teeth are separated so that no driving can take place, and the staggered ramps will not permit teeth engagement, thus preventing the wheel from spinning uncontrollably. [2]

The compound planetary drive train has largely replaced designs using two separate planetary gearsets due to its compactness and ability to provide two forward speeds, reverse, and neutral [1]. When the lockup clutch in the torque converter engages, the power path changes as follows: the converter pump and turbine are locked together and rotate as a single unit. During a steer in neutral range, the output ring gears stay stationary while the sun gears turn in opposite directions because the output ring gears are splined to the cross-drive shaft and cannot turn in opposite directions. Meanwhile, the driven bevel gears, which are driven by the sun gears in opposite directions, cause the planet pinions to rotate and move around the ring gears, thereby rotating the planet carriers. The right planet carrier rotates in a forward direction and the left planet carrier rotates in the reverse direction, as shown. This causes the right output flange to rotate in a forward direction and the left output flange to rotate in the reverse direction. [1]
